name: Decapeptide-12

card.summary: A cosmetic brightening peptide with only small, uncontrolled, multi-product studies behind it.
card.note: Studies tested it inside a system with glycolic acid and sunscreen, so its own effect is unclear.

quick.overview:
Decapeptide-12 is a short peptide sold in cosmetic brightening products for dark spots, melasma and sun-related pigmentation. Small open-label studies report improvement in melasma scores and photodamage grades.
Those studies used a full routine including glycolic acid and sunscreen and had no control group.
quick.mechanism: It is described as inhibiting tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, and has been reported to reduce melanin content. Its size and water solubility limit how well it penetrates skin.
quick.risks: The open-label studies reported good tolerability and no adverse events in the small groups tested. Long-term safety data and independent controlled trials are lacking.

lead: Decapeptide-12 is a ten-amino-acid synthetic peptide, sold under the brand name Lumixyl, that is used in cosmetic skin-brightening products to fade dark spots, melasma and sun-related or post-inflammatory pigmentation [5]. People use it to even out skin tone: the peptide is described as inhibiting tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production, so less pigment forms in the dark areas and the complexion looks more uniform [5][4].

The human evidence consists of small open-label studies in which it was combined with other products rather than tested alone: a 0.01% decapeptide-12 cream used with an antioxidant cleanser, a glycolic-acid moisturiser or lotion and a broad-spectrum sunscreen [1][2]. A 2021 pharmaceutics paper characterises it as safer than hydroquinone in reducing melanin content, with efficacy of more than 50% over 16 weeks of twice-daily treatment, but limited by poor skin penetration because it is hydrophilic and large [4].

Wikipedia describes it as investigated for hyperpigmentation disorders such as melasma and as sold off-label as a skin-lightening product [5]. No controlled trial isolating the peptide is among the studies reviewed here, and no looksmaxxing forum discussion of it was found.

chain: Peptide inhibits tyrosinase, the melanin-making enzyme
Less pigment forms in dark spots and patches
angle.text: Decapeptide-12 is applied as a cream, usually as part of a brightening routine with an antioxidant cleanser, a glycolic-acid product and sunscreen, to fade melasma, sun spots and post-inflammatory marks. In the studies, grades of photodamage and melasma scores improved over 16 to 24 weeks [1][2].

paras: Decapeptide-12 is used in cosmetic products aimed at photodamage-related hyperpigmentation, melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation [1][2][3]. Wikipedia reports that it is also sold off-label as a skin-lightening product [5].

subs.h: Skin conditions it is used for
paras: Melasma is a common disorder causing tan, brown or grey-brown patches, usually on the face; Wikipedia's melasma article describes it as more common in women and in people with darker skin types of African, Asian or Hispanic descent, with triggers including UV exposure, pregnancy, contraceptives and hormone therapy [6]. It describes combination treatment as generally considered most effective, with options including hydroquinone, azelaic acid, kojic acid, alpha arbutin, tranexamic acid, chemical peels and strict sun protection, and calls the condition chronic and relapsing [6]. Decapeptide-12 products are positioned as one option among topical brighteners.

Wikipedia gives the sequence as YRSRKYSSWY, the formula C65H90N18O17 and a molar mass of about 1395.5 g/mol [5]. Because it is a ten-residue hydrophilic peptide, it penetrates skin poorly, which has driven formulation work [4].

It is described as a tyrosinase-inhibiting peptide that reduces melanin content [5][4]. A 2009 study cited by Wikipedia reported that short oligopeptides inhibit both mushroom and human tyrosinase [5]. In the 2021 pharmaceutics study, molecular docking showed that the native peptide and a palmitate-modified version had similar activity towards tyrosinase [4].

Its hydrophilicity and large molecular size limit transcutaneous penetration. Researchers therefore tested adding a palmitate chain, chemical penetration enhancers (oleic acid and menthol) and a microneedle patch in vitro with human skin: the palmitoylated peptide achieved the best skin retention, and permeation of the native peptide improved with the microneedle patch but not the chemical enhancers [4].

Reported effects come from open-label studies of multi-product systems. In the photodamage study, 24 weeks of use was associated with improvement on a photodamage grading scale (38.5 percent of completers cleared from moderate photodamage to none) [1]. In the melasma study of 33 Hispanic women, mean MASI scores fell by 36, 46, 54 and 60 percent at weeks 4, 8, 12 and 16 [2]. A 2014 report examined combined topical delivery and dermal infusion for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in skin of colour [3].

The open-label studies reported the regimens were well tolerated in the small groups tested; the melasma study reported no adverse events [1][2]. Long-term safety data and regulatory documents were not found. Wikipedia's article does not describe side effects [5].
Lumixyl is the brand name given by Wikipedia; Wikipedia's article lists no regulatory details [5]. Wikipedia lists hydroquinone and melanotan II as related reading [5].

In a prospective open-label study of 15 women (13 completed) with Fitzpatrick skin types I-IV and facial hyperpigmentation from chronic photodamage, decapeptide-12 was used with an antioxidant cleanser, a glycolic-acid moisturiser and sunscreen; at 24 weeks 38.5% of participants had cleared from moderate to no photodamage on the grading scale, 30.7% improved from moderate to mild, and 15.4% moved from severe to moderate and another 15.4% from severe to mild. The treatments were reported to be well tolerated [1].

A multicentre open-label study in 33 Hispanic women with mild to moderate melasma used 0.01% decapeptide-12 with an antioxidant cleanser, 20% buffered glycolic acid lotion and SPF 30 sunscreen for 16 weeks; mean decreases in the MASI score were 36%, 46%, 54% and 60% at weeks 4, 8, 12 and 16, with no adverse events reported [2]. A 2014 report examined combined topical delivery and dermal infusion of the peptide for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in skin of colour [3].
All of these studies were uncontrolled and tested multi-component systems, so the contribution of the peptide alone cannot be separated from the glycolic acid and sunscreen they included.
